label: M7 S11 | The Return Formula Stack and the DuPont Decomposition

formulas.name: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
formulas.formula: ROCE = EBIT / Average Capital Employed\nWhere Capital Employed = Shareholders' Equity + Total Debt (Long-term + Short-term)\nOR equivalently: Total Assets − Non-Interest-Bearing Current Liabilities

variables.meaning: Earnings Before Interest and Tax from the P&L. Represents operating profit available to all capital providers before financing and tax decisions.
The total capital invested in operations — equity capital plus interest-bearing debt. Average of opening and closing balances for the period.

formulas.worked_example:
Asian Paints FY24:
EBIT: ₹6,880 cr
Shareholders' Equity (avg): ₹18,620 cr
Total Debt (avg): ₹2,850 cr
Capital Employed (avg): ₹21,470 cr

ROCE = 6,880 / 21,470 = 32.0%

Interpretation: Asian Paints generates ₹32 of pre-tax operating profit for every ₹100 of capital invested in operations. This is among the highest ROCE levels in Indian equity markets, driven by: (a) strong brand-driven pricing power (gross margin 38-42%), (b) efficient working capital management (slightly negative to modestly positive CCC), (c) asset-light manufacturing (shared facilities, outsourced packaging), (d) distribution scale economies (40,000+ dealers).

Peer context (FY24):
• Asian Paints: 32%
• Berger Paints: 18%
• Kansai Nerolac: 15%
• Indigo Paints: 17%

The 14-17 percentage point gap versus peers is the quantitative measure of Asian Paints' franchise strength. Over 10 years, compounding at 30% ROCE versus 15% means total capital earns double the returns — which is why Asian Paints has delivered approximately 25% total-return CAGR over multiple decades.
formulas.sensitivity_note: A 200 bps deterioration in ROCE (30% to 28%) on a ₹21,470 cr capital base represents ₹430 cr of foregone annual earnings — nearly 10% of current EBIT. ROCE deterioration is therefore both a leading indicator of business quality change AND a direct driver of earnings impact.

formulas.name: The DuPont Decomposition of ROE
formulas.formula: ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier\nROE = (Net Income / Revenue) × (Revenue / Average Assets) × (Average Assets / Average Equity)

variables.meaning: Net Income divided by Revenue — measures profitability
Revenue divided by Average Total Assets — measures asset efficiency (how much revenue is generated per rupee of assets)
Average Total Assets divided by Average Equity — measures leverage (how much total assets are supported by each rupee of equity)

formulas.worked_example:
HUL FY24 DuPont Decomposition:
Net Profit Margin: 10,280 / 60,980 = 16.9%
Asset Turnover: 60,980 / 34,580 = 1.76x
Equity Multiplier: 34,580 / 12,050 = 2.87x

ROE = 16.9% × 1.76 × 2.87 = 85.3%

Check: ROE = 10,280 / 12,050 = 85.3% ✓

TCS FY24 DuPont Decomposition:
Net Profit Margin: 46,099 / 240,893 = 19.1%
Asset Turnover: 240,893 / 1,28,200 = 1.88x
Equity Multiplier: 1,28,200 / 98,340 = 1.30x

ROE = 19.1% × 1.88 × 1.30 = 46.7%

INSIGHT: HUL and TCS have similar net profit margins (16.9% vs 19.1%) and similar asset turnover (1.76 vs 1.88). The massive ROE difference (85% vs 47%) is almost entirely explained by the equity multiplier — HUL operates with 2.87x assets to equity (high operating leverage through payables and consumer goods financing), TCS operates with only 1.30x (cash-rich, low-debt IT services structure). This is a leverage-driven ROE difference, not an operational difference. DuPont reveals this clearly where raw ROE comparison misleads.
formulas.sensitivity_note: DuPont decomposition is the most useful tool for understanding WHY two companies have different ROE. Without it, comparing ROE across leverage-different companies is analytically meaningless.

formulas.name: ROIC vs WACC — The Value Creation Test
formulas.formula:
Value Creation = (ROIC − WACC) × Invested Capital
ROIC = NOPAT / Invested Capital
NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − Effective Tax Rate)
WACC = [E/(E+D)] × Cost of Equity + [D/(E+D)] × Cost of Debt × (1 − Tax)

variables.meaning: Net Operating Profit After Tax — operating profit adjusted for tax, excluding interest effects
Equity + Interest-bearing Debt − Excess Cash. Represents the capital actually invested in operations.
The blended cost of capital — typically 11-13% for Indian corporates

formulas.worked_example:
TCS FY24 Value Creation Analysis:
EBIT: ₹55,000 cr
Effective Tax Rate: 25.17%
NOPAT = 55,000 × (1 − 0.2517) = ₹41,157 cr
Equity: ₹98,340 cr
Debt: ₹3,750 cr
Excess Cash: ~₹35,000 cr (TCS is cash-rich)
Invested Capital = 98,340 + 3,750 − 35,000 = ₹67,090 cr
ROIC = 41,157 / 67,090 = 61.3%

WACC for TCS (assume): ~10% (low-risk cash-rich services business)

Value Creation Spread: ROIC − WACC = 61.3% − 10.0% = 51.3 percentage points

Interpretation: TCS earns 51 percentage points above its cost of capital. Over a year, this represents (51.3% × 67,090 cr) = ₹34,400 cr of economic value added. This is why TCS trades at premium multiples — the compounding of 51% spread over WACC creates enormous long-term shareholder value.
formulas.sensitivity_note: Value creation is fundamentally about the spread (ROIC − WACC), not the absolute ROIC. A company earning 15% ROIC vs 12% WACC (3 pp spread) creates more value than a company earning 25% ROIC vs 30% WACC (−5 pp spread). The spread times Invested Capital = economic value added annually.

windows: Alt+N+N → Insert line chart (for multi-year ROCE trend)
Ctrl+D → Fill down (useful for copying ROCE formulas across years)

formulas.name: The DuPont Decomposition of ROE
formulas.formula:
ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
ROE = (Net Income / Revenue) × (Revenue / Average Assets) × (Average Assets / Average Equity)

variables.meaning: Net Income divided by Revenue — measures profitability
Revenue divided by Average Total Assets — measures asset efficiency (how much revenue is generated per rupee of assets)
Average Total Assets divided by Average Equity — measures leverage (how much total assets are supported by each rupee of equity)

formulas.plain_english: DuPont decomposition breaks down ROE into three independent drivers: profitability (how much profit you make per rupee of sales), efficiency (how much revenue you generate per rupee of assets), and leverage (how much you borrow relative to equity). This three-part view reveals the real source of ROE differences — whether two companies have different ROE because of operating margins, asset turns, or leverage decisions. Without DuPont, comparing ROE across companies with different capital structures is analytically misleading.
computation: Calculate Net Profit Margin: Net Income / Revenue
Calculate Asset Turnover: Revenue / Average Total Assets
Calculate Equity Multiplier: Average Total Assets / Average Equity
Multiply all three ratios: Margin × Turnover × Multiplier = ROE
Verify by calculating ROE directly: Net Income / Average Equity (should match)

HUL FY24 — Equity Multiplier: ₹34,580 cr / ₹12,050 cr = 2.87x
HUL ROE direct check: ₹10,280 cr / ₹12,050 cr = 85.3% ✓

TCS FY24 — Asset Turnover: ₹240,893 cr / ₹1,28,200 cr = 1.88x
TCS FY24 — Equity Multiplier: ₹1,28,200 cr / ₹98,340 cr = 1.30x

The massive ROE difference (85% vs 47%) is almost entirely explained by the equity multiplier — HUL operates with 2.87x assets to equity (high operating leverage through payables and consumer goods financing), TCS operates with only 1.30x (cash-rich, low-debt IT services structure). This is a leverage-driven ROE difference, not an operational difference. DuPont reveals this clearly where raw ROE comparison misleads.

formulas.sensitivity_note: DuPont decomposition is the most useful tool for understanding WHY two companies have different ROE. Without it, comparing ROE across leverage-different companies is analytically meaningless.

formulas.name: ROIC vs WACC — The Value Creation Test
formulas.formula:
Value Creation = (ROIC − WACC) × Invested Capital
ROIC = NOPAT / Invested Capital
NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − Effective Tax Rate)
WACC = [E/(E+D)] × Cost of Equity + [D/(E+D)] × Cost of Debt × (1 − Tax)

variables.meaning: Return on Invested Capital — the after-tax return earned on all capital (equity and debt) deployed in operations
Net Operating Profit After Tax — operating profit adjusted for tax, excluding interest effects
Equity + Interest-bearing Debt − Excess Cash. Represents the capital actually invested in operations.
The blended cost of capital — typically 11-13% for Indian corporates
The required return demanded by equity shareholders, typically calculated via CAPM
The weighted average interest rate on borrowed funds

formulas.plain_english: The spread between ROIC and WACC (the spread) is the true measure of whether a company is creating shareholder value. If ROIC exceeds WACC, the business earns more than its cost of capital — surplus value is created. If ROIC falls below WACC, capital is being destroyed. The magnitude of the spread, multiplied by invested capital, equals the economic value added annually. This is why ROIC-WACC analysis is far superior to P/E or P/B for assessing franchise quality — it directly measures whether management is deploying capital productively.
computation: Extract EBIT from the P&L and calculate Effective Tax Rate (Total Tax / EBT)
Calculate NOPAT: EBIT × (1 − Effective Tax Rate)
Sum Shareholders' Equity + Interest-bearing Debt from balance sheet
Deduct Excess Cash (typically hold at least 2-3% of revenue for operations)
Invested Capital = Equity + Debt − Excess Cash
Estimate WACC using market data (Cost of Equity from CAPM, Cost of Debt from bond yields or borrowing rates, tax rate, capital structure proportions)
Economic Value Added (annual): Spread × Invested Capital

worked_example.problem: Calculate ROIC, WACC, and value creation spread for TCS FY24 to assess how much economic value is being created annually.
steps: Total Tax / EBT: Effective Tax Rate = 25.17%
Invested Capital = ₹98,340 cr + ₹3,750 cr − ₹35,000 cr = ₹67,090 cr
WACC for TCS (estimated based on low-risk cash-rich services business profile): ~10.0%
worked_example.result: ROIC: 61.3%; WACC: 10.0%; Spread: 51.3 pp; Annual EVA: ₹34,400 cr
worked_example.insight: TCS earns 51 percentage points above its cost of capital. Over a year, this represents ₹34,400 cr of economic value added. This is why TCS trades at premium multiples — the compounding of 51% spread over WACC creates enormous long-term shareholder value. In contrast, a lower-quality business earning 15% ROIC against a 12% WACC (3 pp spread) creates substantially less EVA. The ROIC-WACC framework shows that franchise quality is ultimately about earning multiples above your cost of capital, not absolute ROIC alone.

formulas.sensitivity_note: Value creation is fundamentally about the spread (ROIC − WACC), not the absolute ROIC. A company earning 15% ROIC vs 12% WACC (3 pp spread) creates more value than a company earning 25% ROIC vs 30% WACC (−5 pp spread). The spread times Invested Capital = economic value added annually.
